claim: Brief (1 hr) periods of postsynaptic bursting selectively depressed AMPA receptor (R) synaptic transmission.
source: Brief (1 hr) periods of postsynaptic bursting selectively depressed AMPA receptor (R) synaptic transmission, or silenced excitatory synapses, whereas more prolonged (24 hr) firing depressed both AMPAR and NMDAR EPSCs and eliminated spines, indicative of a synapse elimination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing depression of AMPAR EPSCs after brief PPS in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Brief (1 hr) periods of postsynaptic bursting silenced excitatory synapses.
source: Brief (1 hr) periods of postsynaptic bursting selectively depressed AMPA receptor (R) synaptic transmission, or silenced excitatory synapses, whereas more prolonged (24 hr) firing depressed both AMPAR and NMDAR EPSCs and eliminated spines, indicative of a synapse elimination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing selective depression of AMPAR but not NMDAR EPSCs after brief PPS.

claim: Prolonged (24 hr) firing depressed both AMPAR and NMDAR EPSCs.
source: Brief (1 hr) periods of postsynaptic bursting selectively depressed AMPA receptor (R) synaptic transmission, or silenced excitatory synapses, whereas more prolonged (24 hr) firing depressed both AMPAR and NMDAR EPSCs and eliminated spines, indicative of a synapse elimination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2C and 2D showing depression of both AMPAR and NMDAR EPSCs after chronic PPS.

claim: Prolonged (24 hr) firing eliminated spines, indicative of synapse elimination.
source: Brief (1 hr) periods of postsynaptic bursting selectively depressed AMPA receptor (R) synaptic transmission, or silenced excitatory synapses, whereas more prolonged (24 hr) firing depressed both AMPAR and NMDAR EPSCs and eliminated spines, indicative of a synapse elimination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2F showing reduced spine density after chronic PPS.

claim: Both synapse silencing and elimination required de novo transcription.
source: Both synapse silencing and elimination required de novo transcription, but only silencing required the activity-dependent transcription factors MEF2A/D.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that transcription inhibitors DRB and ActD blocked PPS-induced synaptic depression.

claim: Only synapse silencing required the activity-dependent transcription factors MEF2A/D.
source: Both synapse silencing and elimination required de novo transcription, but only silencing required the activity-dependent transcription factors MEF2A/D.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that MEF2A/D deletion blocked brief PPS-induced synaptic depression but not chronic PPS-induced depression.

claim: Burst firing induced MEF2A/D-dependent induction of the target gene Arc.
source: Burst firing induced MEF2A/D-dependent induction of the target gene Arc which contributed to synapse silencing and elimination.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 6A showing Arc induction by PPS that is abolished in MEF2A/D KO cultures.

claim: Arc contributed to synapse silencing and elimination.
source: Burst firing induced MEF2A/D-dependent induction of the target gene Arc which contributed to synapse silencing and elimination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that Arc KO neurons failed to show PPS-induced synaptic depression.

claim: Sensory experience and learning refine cortical circuits through synapse elimination.
source: Sensory experience and learning refine cortical circuits through activity-dependent stabilization and elimination of excitatory synaptic connections (Hua and Smith, 2004; Zuo et al., 2005; Fu and Zuo, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Deficits in experience-dependent synapse elimination are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, such as Fragile X Syndrome, autism and schizophrenia.
source: Importantly, deficits in experience-dependent synapse elimination are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, such as Fragile X Syndrome, autism and schizophrenia (Pfeiffer et al., 2010; Patel et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2014; Nagaoka et al., 2016; Sekar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activity- and experience-regulated transcriptional control is a candidate mechanism to transduce activity signals into long-term changes in circuit connectivity.
source: Activity- and experience-regulated transcriptional control is a candidate mechanism to transduce activity signals into long-term changes in circuit connectivity (Flavell and Greenberg, 2008; West and Greenberg, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The MEF2 family of activity-dependent transcription factors has been implicated in functional and structural elimination of excitatory synapses.
source: In support of this idea, the MEF2 (Myocyte-Enhancer Factor 2) family of activity-dependent transcription factors has been implicated in functional and structural elimination of excitatory synapses (Flavell et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: All four MEF2 family members (MEF2A-D) are expressed in the brain.
source: All four MEF2 family members (MEF2A-D) are expressed in the brain.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: MEF2A and MEF2D are highly expressed in hippocampal CA1 neurons.
source: MEF2A and MEF2D are highly expressed in hippocampal CA1 neurons and MEF2C is expressed more in the dentate gyrus and neocortex (Lyons et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: MEF2C is expressed more in the dentate gyrus and neocortex.
source: MEF2A and MEF2D are highly expressed in hippocampal CA1 neurons and MEF2C is expressed more in the dentate gyrus and neocortex (Lyons et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: MEF2C and MEF2D as well as MEF2 target genes, are implicated in human autism, intellectual disability, schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease and/or epilepsy.
source: MEF2C and MEF2D as well as MEF2 target genes, are implicated in human autism, intellectual disability, schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease and/or epilepsy (Rocha et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In mice, deletion of Mef2a,c, and/or d leads to behaviors relevant to autism and drug addiction and alterations in learning and memory.
source: In mice, deletion of Mef2a,c, and/or d leads to behaviors relevant to autism and drug addiction and alterations in learning and memory (Pulipparacharuvil et al., 2008; Cole et al., 2012; Harrington et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MEF2-VP16 expression causes rapid elimination of excitatory synapses in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: MEF2-VP16 expression causes rapid elimination of excitatory synapses in cultured hippocampal neurons (Flavell et al., 2006; Pfeiffer et al., 2010; Wilkerson et al., 2014) and in vivo (Barbosa et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MEF2-VP16 expression causes rapid elimination of excitatory synapses in vivo.
source: MEF2-VP16 expression causes rapid elimination of excitatory synapses in cultured hippocampal neurons (Flavell et al., 2006; Pfeiffer et al., 2010; Wilkerson et al., 2014) and in vivo (Barbosa et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MEF2C knockout mice display enhanced spine number and excitatory synaptic function of dentate gyrus granule cells.
source: In support of a role for endogenous MEF2 genes in synapse elimination, MEF2C knockout mice display enhanced spine number and excitatory synaptic function of dentate gyrus granule cells (Barbosa et al., 2008) and knockdown of MEF2A/D in hippocampal cultures increases excitatory synapse markers, an effect that relies on activity of the cultures (Flavell et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Knockdown of MEF2A/D in hippocampal cultures increases excitatory synapse markers, an effect that relies on activity of the cultures.
source: In support of a role for endogenous MEF2 genes in synapse elimination, MEF2C knockout mice display enhanced spine number and excitatory synaptic function of dentate gyrus granule cells (Barbosa et al., 2008) and knockdown of MEF2A/D in hippocampal cultures increases excitatory synapse markers, an effect that relies on activity of the cultures (Flavell et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: MEF2A/D knockdown does not always lead to increases in synapse number.
source: However, MEF2A/D knockdown does not always lead to increases in synapse number (Akhtar et al., 2012; Elmer et al., 2013) suggesting there may be specific activity patterns or other factors necessary to observe MEF2A/D dependent synaptic plasticity.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CA1 neurons fire in bursts at a theta frequency (3–8 Hz) in vivo during novel environment exploration and learning.
source: CA1 neurons fire in bursts at a theta frequency (3–8 Hz) in vivo during novel environment exploration and learning (Colgin, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Chronic, 24 hr, bursting of CA1 neurons at 3 Hz resulted in elimination of excitatory synapses.
source: Using optogenetics to drive individual CA1 neurons in organotypic rat hippocampal slice cultures, Goold and Nicoll (2010) observed that chronic, 24 hr, bursting of CA1 neurons at 3 Hz (Figure 1A) resulted in elimination of excitatory synapses.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Transfected neurons exposed to 1 hr (brief) PPS displayed a robust (~50%) depression of evoked EPSC amplitude relative to untransfected neurons.
source: Transfected neurons exposed to 1 hr (brief) PPS displayed a robust (~50%) depression of evoked EPSC amplitude and mEPSC frequency relative to untransfected neurons (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Transfected neurons exposed to 1 hr (brief) PPS displayed a robust depression of mEPSC frequency relative to untransfected neurons.
source: Transfected neurons exposed to 1 hr (brief) PPS displayed a robust (~50%) depression of evoked EPSC amplitude and mEPSC frequency relative to untransfected neurons (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Brief PPS did not affect mEPSC amplitude.
source: In contrast, mEPSC amplitude and paired pulse facilitation of evoked EPSCs were unaffected (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Brief PPS did not affect paired pulse facilitation of evoked EPSCs.
source: In contrast, mEPSC amplitude and paired pulse facilitation of evoked EPSCs were unaffected (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Transfection of ChR2, without PPS, had no effect on any measure of synaptic function.
source: As a control, transfection of ChR2, without PPS, had no effect on any measure of synaptic function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Longer durations of PPS (6 or 24 hr; chronic PPS) also depressed evoked EPSCs and mEPSC frequency.
source: Longer durations of PPS (6 or 24 hr; chronic PPS) also depressed evoked EPSCs and mEPSC frequency (measured 24 hr after PPS onset, Figure 1D), without affecting mEPSC amplitude or paired-pulse facilitation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Chronic PPS did not affect mEPSC amplitude or paired-pulse facilitation.
source: Longer durations of PPS (6 or 24 hr; chronic PPS) also depressed evoked EPSCs and mEPSC frequency (measured 24 hr after PPS onset, Figure 1D), without affecting mEPSC amplitude or paired-pulse facilitation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Chronic PPS or expression of MEF2VP16 in CA1 neurons causes a functional and structural elimination of synapses that manifests as depressed EPSCs and mEPSC frequency without changes in mEPSC amplitude or paired-pulse facilitation.
source: Chronic PPS or expression of MEF2VP16 in CA1 neurons causes a functional and structural elimination of synapses that manifests as depressed EPSCs and mEPSC frequency without changes in mEPSC amplitude or paired-pulse facilitation (Goold and Nicoll, 2010; Pfeiffer et al., 2010; Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Brief PPS suppressed evoked AMPAR EPSCs but had no effect on NMDAR EPSCs recorded 24–30 hr after the onset of PPS.
source: Although brief PPS suppressed evoked AMPAR EPSCs, it had no effect on NMDAR EPSCs recorded 24–30 hr after the onset of PPS (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Brief PPS induced a selective depression of AMPAR, but not NMDAR EPSCs at 3–7 or 12–16 hr after PPS onset.
source: To determine if NMDAR EPSCs are initially depressed by brief PPS, but recover after PPS offset, we measured AMPA and NMDAR EPSCs at earlier time points after brief PPS onset, either 3–7 or 12–16 hr, and observed a selective depression of AMPAR, but not NMDAR EPSCs (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Synapses with NMDARs, but not AMPARs are referred to as 'silent' synapses.
source: Synapses with NMDARs, but not AMPARs are referred to as 'silent' synapses (Kawashima et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Brief PPS appears to silence excitatory synapses.
source: Thus, brief PPS appears to silence excitatory synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the selective depression of AMPAR but not NMDAR EPSCs.

claim: Chronic PPS depressed both AMPAR and NMDAR EPSCs, recorded at either 24–30 or 48–54 hr after the onset of chronic PPS.
source: In contrast, chronic PPS depressed both AMPAR and NMDAR EPSCs, recorded at either 24–30 or 48–54 hr (Figure 2C,D, Supplementary file 1) after the onset of chronic PPS, consistent with a functional synapse elimination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Brief PPS had no effect on spine density.
source: Brief PPS had no effect on spine density (Figure 2E), consistent with a functional synapse silencing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Chronic PPS reduced spine density on secondary apical dendrites, compared to transfected neurons without PPS.
source: In contrast, chronic PPS reduced spine density on secondary apical dendrites, compared to transfected neurons without PPS (Figure 2F) which, together with our functional measurements indicate that chronic PPS eliminates synapses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Chronic PPS of neurons transfected with GFP alone had no effect on spine number.
source: As a control, chronic PPS of neurons transfected with GFP alone had no effect on spine number, indicating that decreased spine density was a result of light driven ChR2 activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PPS stimulation for 1–24 hr robustly induced the MRE-GFP reporter.
source: However, PPS stimulation for 1–24 hr robustly induced the MRE-GFP reporter (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Deletion or knockout (KO) of MEF2A/D blocked MRE-GFP induction in response to brief (1 hr) and chronic (24 hr) PPS.
source: Deletion or knockout (KO) of MEF2A/D blocked MRE-GFP induction in response to brief (1 hr) and chronic (24 hr) PPS (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: MEF2A/D KO did not affect ChR2 expression, as assessed by blue light-induced currents.
source: MEF2A/D KO did not affect ChR2 expression, as assessed by blue light-induced currents (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Physiological action potential patterns activate MEF2A/D-driven transcriptional activation.
source: These results indicate that physiological action potential patterns activate MEF2A/D-driven transcriptional activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PPS induces MRE-GFP in a MEF2A/D-dependent manner.

claim: MEF2A/D deletion had no effect on evoked or mEPSCs in unstimulated cultures (no PPS).
source: MEF2A/D deletion, without PPS, had no effect on evoked or mEPSCs in unstimulated cultures (no PPS; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), but blocked the ability of brief PPS (1 hr) to depress EPSCs and mEPSC frequency (Figure 4A,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MEF2A/D deletion blocked the ability of brief PPS (1 hr) to depress EPSCs and mEPSC frequency.
source: MEF2A/D deletion, without PPS, had no effect on evoked or mEPSCs in unstimulated cultures (no PPS; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), but blocked the ability of brief PPS (1 hr) to depress EPSCs and mEPSC frequency (Figure 4A,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4D.

claim: MEF2A/D KO neurons had normal synaptic depression induced by chronic PPS.
source: In contrast to our results with brief PPS, MEF2A/D KO neurons had normal synaptic depression induced by chronic PPS (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4D.

claim: 6 hr of PPS in MEF2A/D KO neurons induced only a trend towards a depressed evoked EPSC amplitude compared to WT.
source: Compared to WT, 6 hr of PPS in MEF2A/D KO neurons induced only a trend towards a depressed evoked EPSC amplitude (Figure 4C,D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Chronic PPS induced a persistent depression of AMPA and NMDAR EPSCs in neurons with MEF2A/D deletion.
source: Similar to WT, chronic PPS induced a persistent depression of AMPA and NMDAR EPSCs in neurons with MEF2A/D deletion, (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1), supporting a specific role for MEF2A/D in synapse silencing in response to brief PPS.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Neuronal depolarization drives MEF2A/D-mediated transcriptional activation by activating L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCC) and subsequent Ca2+ influx.
source: Neuronal depolarization drives MEF2A/D-mediated transcriptional activation by activating L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCC) and subsequent Ca2+ influx (Flavell et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Nifedipine blocked brief PPS-induced MRE-GFP.
source: However, nifedipine blocked brief PPS-induced MRE-GFP (Figure 5A,B) as well as depression of evoked EPSCs and mEPSC frequency (Figure 5C) without affecting expression or function of ChR2 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Nifedipine blocked brief PPS-induced depression of evoked EPSCs and mEPSC frequency.
source: However, nifedipine blocked brief PPS-induced MRE-GFP (Figure 5A,B) as well as depression of evoked EPSCs and mEPSC frequency (Figure 5C) without affecting expression or function of ChR2 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: DRB blocked PPS-induced expression of MRE-GFP.
source: As expected, DRB blocked PPS-induced expression of MRE-GFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B) and depression of mEPSC frequency (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: DRB blocked PPS-induced depression of mEPSC frequency.
source: As expected, DRB blocked PPS-induced expression of MRE-GFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B) and depression of mEPSC frequency (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Actinomycin D (ActD) blocked brief PPS-induced depression of mEPSC frequency.
source: Another transcription inhibitor with a distinct mode of action; actinomycin D (ActD; 1 µM; Figure 5E), also blocked brief PPS-induced depression of mEPSC frequency.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Anisomycin blocked chronic PPS induced depression of evoked and mEPSCs.
source: Therefore, we tested the translation inhibitor, anisomycin (20 µM), which blocked chronic PPS induced depression of evoked and mEPSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Arc was robustly induced (~20 fold) by the patterned postsynaptic bursting (brief PPS), at 3, 6 and 12 hr after PPS onset.
source: Arc was robustly induced (~20 fold) by the patterned postsynaptic bursting (brief PPS), at 3, 6 and 12 hr after PPS onset (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; n = 3–5 cultures).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Brief PPS did not induce Rgs2 or Pcdh10.
source: Brief PPS did not induce Rgs2 or Pcdh10 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and 1E.

claim: Mef2a/d deletion abolished PPS-induced Arc expression at all time points assayed.
source: Mef2a/d deletion abolished PPS-induced Arc expression at all time points assayed (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Physiological patterns of postsynaptic bursting selectively induce a subset of MEF2A/D target genes.
source: These results suggest physiological patterns of postsynaptic bursting selectively induce a subset of MEF2A/D target genes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PPS induces Arc but not other MEF2 target genes.

claim: Brief PPS failed to induce depression of AMPAR EPSCs or mEPSC frequency in Arc KO neurons in comparison to WT littermate controls.
source: In support of our hypothesis, brief PPS failed to induce depression of AMPAR EPSCs or mEPSC frequency in Arc KO neurons in comparison to WT littermate controls (Figure 6B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Arc cDNA expression in unstimulated cultures, without PPS, did not affect evoked EPSCs or mEPSCs.
source: Arc cDNA expression in unstimulated cultures, without PPS, did not affect evoked EPSCs or mEPSCs (Figure 6C1, Supplementary file 1), indicating that expression of Arc alone is not sufficient to silence synapses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C1.

claim: Expression of Arc alone is not sufficient to silence synapses.
source: Arc cDNA expression in unstimulated cultures, without PPS, did not affect evoked EPSCs or mEPSCs (Figure 6C1, Supplementary file 1), indicating that expression of Arc alone is not sufficient to silence synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Arc expression without PPS does not affect synaptic function.

claim: Arc cDNA expression in Arc KO neurons that received brief PPS rescued depression of evoked EPSCs and mEPSC frequency.
source: However, Arc cDNA expression in Arc KO neurons that received brief PPS rescued depression of evoked EPSCs and mEPSC frequency (Figure 6C2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C2.

claim: Exogenous expression of Arc in MEF2A/D-KO neurons had no effect on mEPSCs in unstimulated cultures and failed to rescue PPS-induced synapse silencing.
source: Exogenous expression of Arc in MEF2A/D-KO neurons had no effect on mEPSCs in unstimulated cultures and failed to rescue PPS-induced synapse silencing (Figure 6D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Exogenous Arc can rescue PPS-induced synapse silencing in Arc KO neurons, but not MEF2A/D KO neurons.
source: Therefore, exogenous Arc can rescue PPS-induced synapse silencing in Arc KO neurons, but not MEF2A/D KO neurons, implicating other activity- and MEF2A/D-dependent gene targets in synapse silencing, in addition to Arc.
evidence: Inferred from the differential rescue effects of Arc in Arc KO vs MEF2A/D KO neurons.

claim: Other activity- and MEF2A/D-dependent gene targets are implicated in synapse silencing, in addition to Arc.
source: Therefore, exogenous Arc can rescue PPS-induced synapse silencing in Arc KO neurons, but not MEF2A/D KO neurons, implicating other activity- and MEF2A/D-dependent gene targets in synapse silencing, in addition to Arc.
evidence: Inferred from the failure of Arc to rescue PPS-induced silencing in MEF2A/D KO neurons.

claim: Chronic PPS failed to depress mEPSCs in Arc KO neurons.
source: Chronic PPS failed to depress mEPSCs in Arc KO neurons and the depression of evoked EPSCs was quantitatively less in Arc KO neurons compared to WT littermates (Figure 6E, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The depression of evoked EPSCs by chronic PPS was quantitatively less in Arc KO neurons compared to WT littermates.
source: Chronic PPS failed to depress mEPSCs in Arc KO neurons and the depression of evoked EPSCs was quantitatively less in Arc KO neurons compared to WT littermates (Figure 6E, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Arc is essential for synaptic silencing and contributes quantitatively to synapse elimination in response to PPS.
source: Thus, Arc is essential for synaptic silencing and contributes quantitatively to synapse elimination in response to PPS.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Arc KO blocks silencing and partially blocks elimination.

claim: Other transcription factors that mediate activity-induced Arc may contribute to synapse elimination or can compensate for loss of MEF2A/D.
source: Other transcription factors that mediate activity-induced Arc (Kawashima et al., 2009) may contribute to synapse elimination or can compensate for loss of MEF2A/D.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: Different durations or levels of intracellular Ca2+ increases may engage different transcription factors and gene expression programs to homeostatically depress synaptic function through distinct mechanisms.
source: Thus, different durations or levels of intracellular Ca2+ increases may engage different transcription factors and gene expression programs to homeostatically depress synaptic function through distinct mechanisms.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the differential requirements for MEF2A/D in brief vs chronic PPS.

claim: Brief (~1 hr) PPS caused a decrease in mEPSC frequency and evoked AMPAR-EPSCs without affecting NMDAR-EPSCs, dendritic spine number or paired-pulse facilitation of evoked EPSCs.
source: Brief (~1 hr) PPS caused a decrease in mEPSC frequency and evoked AMPAR-EPSCs without affecting NMDAR-EPSCs, dendritic spine number or paired-pulse facilitation of evoked EPSCs, a measure related to presynaptic release probability.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Brief PPS causes a removal or inactivation of all AMPARs, at a subset of synapses, or creates silent synapses.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that brief PPS causes a removal or inactivation of all AMPARs, at a subset of synapses, or creates silent synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the selective depression of AMPAR but not NMDAR EPSCs without changes in spine number.

claim: Chronic PPS (~24 hr) also depressed the frequency of mEPSCs, but in contrast to brief PPS, depressed both evoked AMPA and NMDAR-mediated EPSCs and reduced spine number without affecting paired-pulse facilitation.
source: Chronic PPS (~24 hr) also depressed the frequency of mEPSCs, but in contrast to brief PPS, depressed both evoked AMPA and NMDAR-mediated EPSCs and reduced spine number without affecting paired-pulse facilitation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Figure 2.

claim: Brief or chronic PPS did not affect the average amplitude of mEPSCs.
source: Because brief or chronic PPS did not affect the average amplitude of mEPSCs, this suggests that synapses are silenced and eliminated across a range of synaptic strengths.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Supplementary file 1.

claim: Synapses are silenced and eliminated across a range of synaptic strengths.
source: Because brief or chronic PPS did not affect the average amplitude of mEPSCs, this suggests that synapses are silenced and eliminated across a range of synaptic strengths.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect on mEPSC amplitude.

claim: The synaptic basis of this 'cell autonomous' homeostatic plasticity is distinct from the well characterized homeostatic 'scaling' down of mEPSC amplitudes observed with increased network activity.
source: The synaptic basis of this 'cell autonomous' homeostatic plasticity is distinct from the well characterized homeostatic 'scaling' down of mEPSC amplitudes observed with increased network activity, which results from removal or inactivation of a proportion of AMPARs from all synapses (Wayman et al., 2008; Vitureira et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by comparison to previous literature on homeostatic scaling.

claim: Homeostatic scaling maintains the relative synaptic weights of synaptic inputs onto a neuron.
source: While homeostatic scaling maintains the relative synaptic weights of synaptic inputs onto a neuron (Wayman et al., 2008), cell autonomous homeostatic silencing would be expected to eliminate some synaptic inputs, while leaving others unchanged.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cell autonomous homeostatic silencing would be expected to eliminate some synaptic inputs, while leaving others unchanged.
source: While homeostatic scaling maintains the relative synaptic weights of synaptic inputs onto a neuron (Wayman et al., 2008), cell autonomous homeostatic silencing would be expected to eliminate some synaptic inputs, while leaving others unchanged.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanism of cell autonomous homeostatic silencing.

claim: These two forms of homeostatic plasticity (cell autonomous vs. network) would have distinct effects on neural network connectivity and computation and may serve divergent functions.
source: Therefore, these two forms of homeostatic plasticity (cell autonomous vs. network) would have distinct effects on neural network connectivity and computation and may serve divergent functions.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the functional implications of different forms of homeostatic plasticity.

claim: Brief and chronic PPS both require L-type Ca2+ channel activity and transcriptional activation for synapse silencing and elimination.
source: Brief and chronic PPS both require L-type Ca2+ channel activity and transcriptional activation (Goold and Nicoll, 2010) for synapse silencing and elimination, but MEF2A/D is only required for brief PPS-induced synapse silencing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Figure 5 and citation to previous literature.

claim: Brief PPS induced the MRE-GFP transcriptional reporter and target gene Arc, in a MEF2A/D-dependent manner.
source: Consistently, brief PPS induced the MRE-GFP transcriptional reporter and target gene Arc, in a MEF2A/D-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Figures 3 and 6.

claim: Knockdown of MEF2A/D in developing cultured cortical neurons enhanced synaptic expression of GluA1, but not pre-or postsynaptic markers.
source: Consistent with this result, knockdown of MEF2A/D in developing cultured cortical neurons enhanced synaptic expression of GluA1, but not pre-or postsynaptic markers (Elmer et al., 2013), suggesting that endogenous MEF2A/D promotes synaptic removal or endocytosis of GluA1-containing AMPARs.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Endogenous MEF2A/D promotes synaptic removal or endocytosis of GluA1-containing AMPARs.
source: Consistent with this result, knockdown of MEF2A/D in developing cultured cortical neurons enhanced synaptic expression of GluA1, but not pre-or postsynaptic markers (Elmer et al., 2013), suggesting that endogenous MEF2A/D promotes synaptic removal or endocytosis of GluA1-containing AMPARs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MEF2A/D knockdown increases synaptic GluA1.

claim: Postsynaptic deletion of MEF2A/D in CA1 neurons in slice culture did not affect baseline synaptic function.
source: Surprisingly, postsynaptic deletion of MEF2A/D in CA1 neurons in slice culture did not affect baseline synaptic function.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Under basal activity conditions in slice cultures, MEF2A/D is not actively repressing transcription of genes that depress or eliminate synapses, but can be recruited by neural activity to induce transcription of gene targets, such as Arc, that silence synapses.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that under basal activity conditions in slice cultures, MEF2A/D is not actively repressing transcription of genes that depress or eliminate synapses, but can be recruited by neural activity to induce transcription of gene targets, such as Arc, that silence synapses (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of MEF2A/D deletion on baseline synaptic function but requirement for activity-induced silencing.

claim: Chronic PPS-induced synapse elimination relies on transcription and CaMKIV, a known regulator of activity-dependent transcription.
source: Chronic PPS-induced synapse elimination relies on transcription and CaMKIV, a known regulator of activity-dependent transcription (Wayman et al., 2008; Goold and Nicoll, 2010), and, as we demonstrate, quantitatively on Arc.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature and experimental data from Figure 6E.

claim: It is unlikely that compensation by MEF2C occurs with MEF2A/D deletion, because MEF2C is not expressed in CA1 pyramidal neurons postnatally.
source: It is unlikely that compensation by MEF2C occurs with MEF2A/D deletion, because MEF2C is not expressed in CA1 pyramidal neurons postnatally (Lyons et al., 1995; Kamme et al., 2003) and MEF2A/D deletion fully prevented chronic PPS-induced MRE-GFP reporter expression.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature and experimental data from Figure 3.

claim: MEF2A/D deletion fully prevented chronic PPS-induced MRE-GFP reporter expression.
source: It is unlikely that compensation by MEF2C occurs with MEF2A/D deletion, because MEF2C is not expressed in CA1 pyramidal neurons postnatally (Lyons et al., 1995; Kamme et al., 2003) and MEF2A/D deletion fully prevented chronic PPS-induced MRE-GFP reporter expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Figure 3.

claim: CA1 neurons fire in bursts at a theta frequency (3–8 Hz) during exploratory or orienting behavior, as well as REM sleep.
source: CA1 neurons fire in bursts at a theta frequency (3–8 Hz) during exploratory or orienting behavior, as well as REM sleep (Colgin, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Postsynaptic bursting at 3 Hz induced MEF2A/D dependent transcription of Arc and synaptic depression which may contribute to synaptic plasticity during these behaviors.
source: Postsynaptic bursting at 3 Hz induced MEF2A/D dependent transcription of Arc and synaptic depression which may contribute to synaptic plasticity during these behaviors.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the potential behavioral relevance of the findings.

claim: Brief PPS did not induce other MEF2A/D gene targets, such as Pcdh10, Homer1a, and Rgs2, which are induced by MEF2VP16 or high KCl depolarization.
source: Surprisingly, brief PPS did not induce other MEF2A/D gene targets, such as Pcdh10, Homer1a, and Rgs2, which are induced by MEF2VP16 or high KCl depolarization (Flavell et al., 2008), suggesting that other activity patterns may also engage MEF2A/D to induce these genes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous literature.

claim: Other activity patterns may also engage MEF2A/D to induce genes such as Pcdh10, Homer1a, and Rgs2.
source: Surprisingly, brief PPS did not induce other MEF2A/D gene targets, such as Pcdh10, Homer1a, and Rgs2, which are induced by MEF2VP16 or high KCl depolarization (Flavell et al., 2008), suggesting that other activity patterns may also engage MEF2A/D to induce these genes.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the selective induction of Arc by PPS.

claim: Arc promotes endocytosis of AMPARs.
source: Arc promotes endocytosis of AMPARs (Chowdhury et al., 2006; Shepherd et al., 2006) and may do so through interactions of the AMPAR-interacting protein stargazin (TARPγ2) (Penley et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Arc may promote endocytosis of AMPARs through interactions of the AMPAR-interacting protein stargazin (TARPγ2).
source: Arc promotes endocytosis of AMPARs (Chowdhury et al., 2006; Shepherd et al., 2006) and may do so through interactions of the AMPAR-interacting protein stargazin (TARPγ2) (Penley et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Postsynaptic exogenous expression of Arc was not sufficient to cause synaptic depression or elimination.
source: However, postsynaptic exogenous expression of Arc was not sufficient to cause synaptic depression or elimination (Wilkerson et al., 2014), but rescued PPS-induced synaptic depression in Arc KO CA1 neurons.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature and experimental data from Figure 6C.

claim: Arc rescued PPS-induced synaptic depression in Arc KO CA1 neurons.
source: However, postsynaptic exogenous expression of Arc was not sufficient to cause synaptic depression or elimination (Wilkerson et al., 2014), but rescued PPS-induced synaptic depression in Arc KO CA1 neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Figure 6C2.

claim: Other activity-induced, MEF2A/D dependent gene targets, in addition to Arc, are likely necessary to silence synapses.
source: Therefore, other activity-induced, MEF2A/D dependent gene targets, in addition to Arc, are likely necessary to silence synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the failure of Arc alone to rescue silencing in MEF2A/D KO neurons.

claim: Arc is required for MEF2VP16-induced synapse elimination.
source: Consistent with this finding, Arc is required for MEF2VP16-induced synapse elimination (Wilkerson et al., 2014) and developmental and activity-induced elimination of climbing fiber axons onto cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Mikuni et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Arc is required for developmental and activity-induced elimination of climbing fiber axons onto cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: Consistent with this finding, Arc is required for MEF2VP16-induced synapse elimination (Wilkerson et al., 2014) and developmental and activity-induced elimination of climbing fiber axons onto cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Mikuni et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Arc overexpression is not sufficient eliminate climbing fibers.
source: Similar to what we observe in CA1, Arc overexpression is not sufficient eliminate climbing fibers (Mikuni et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Arc-mediated synapse silencing may precede and target synapses for elimination during chronic activity increases.
source: Arc-mediated synapse silencing may precede and target synapses for elimination during chronic activity increases.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the relationship between silencing and elimination.

claim: Silencing and elimination may be distinct processes that both utilize Arc.
source: Alternatively, silencing and elimination may be distinct processes that both utilize Arc.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the relationship between silencing and elimination.

claim: Arc interacts with a number of synaptic proteins, including GluN2A, GluN2B, GKAP and WAVE1.
source: Arc interacts with a number of synaptic proteins, including GluN2A, GluN2B, GKAP and WAVE1 (Penley et al., 2013), through which it may function to depress NMDAR function or spine number, independent of its effects on AMPARs.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Arc may function to depress NMDAR function or spine number, independent of its effects on AMPARs.
source: Arc interacts with a number of synaptic proteins, including GluN2A, GluN2B, GKAP and WAVE1 (Penley et al., 2013), through which it may function to depress NMDAR function or spine number, independent of its effects on AMPARs.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms of Arc function.

claim: MEF2A/D is required for synapse silencing, but not elimination, supporting the idea that silencing is not necessary for elimination.
source: Because MEF2A/D is required for synapse silencing, but not elimination, this supports the idea that silencing is not necessary for elimination.
evidence: Inferred from the differential requirement for MEF2A/D in silencing vs elimination.

claim: Alterations in synaptic pruning or cortical neurons, either during development, in response to experience or with aging are associated with a number of neuropsychiatric diseases, including autism, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Alterations in synaptic pruning or cortical neurons, either during development, in response to experience or with aging are associated with a number of neuropsychiatric diseases, including autism, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease (Tang et al., 2014; Sekar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The intellectual disability and autism-related gene, FMR1, mutated in Fragile X Syndrome, is necessary for developmental and experience-dependent synaptic pruning.
source: For example, the intellectual disability and autism-related gene, FMR1, mutated in Fragile X Syndrome, is necessary for developmental and experience-dependent synaptic pruning (Patel et al., 2014; Nagaoka et al., 2016) as well as pruning in response to MEF2VP16 (Pfeiffer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FMR1 is necessary for pruning in response to MEF2VP16.
source: For example, the intellectual disability and autism-related gene, FMR1, mutated in Fragile X Syndrome, is necessary for developmental and experience-dependent synaptic pruning (Patel et al., 2014; Nagaoka et al., 2016) as well as pruning in response to MEF2VP16 (Pfeiffer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: This work defines distinct stages of activity-regulated synapse elimination.
source: This work defines distinct stages of activity-regulated synapse elimination and provides a reduced and accessible preparation to determine the disease-related mechanisms in cortical synaptic pruning.
evidence: Supported by the experimental findings showing distinct stages of silencing and elimination.

claim: This work provides a reduced and accessible preparation to determine the disease-related mechanisms in cortical synaptic pruning.
